output:
*Interview with Madame Odile Monnier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Madame, thank you for waiting. I know you have been patient. Please sit wherever you are most comfortable.

MME MONNIER: I am comfortable where I am, Inspector. Ask what you need to ask.

MATTHEY: Let us begin at dinner. Tell me what happened when the temple bell struck nine.

MME MONNIER: My husband stood up and asked everyone to show their watches. He did it every year. He liked to know whose watch was keeping time and whose was not, and then he told each owner what was wrong with it.

MATTHEY: Did he speak to everyone in the same way?

MME MONNIER: Not at all. Félix's watch showed twenty minutes to nine, and my husband scolded him for it in front of everyone. Félix laughed and said it was his father's watch and was entitled to its opinions. My husband did not find that amusing. He has never found anything about that watch amusing.

MATTHEY: Why is that?

MME MONNIER: Jules's watch has run badly for ten years, and Félix has never let anyone touch it. Not even Aurèle, and Aurèle would have touched it gladly. It was a point of pride between them, though I could never tell whose pride it was.

MATTHEY: And after dinner?

MME MONNIER: The doctor and I went into the salon and played piquet. We played without a break. Dr Vauthier is the best piquet player I know, which is not saying a great deal, since I know very few. The temple struck ten while we were playing, and we went on.

MATTHEY: You have known Dr Vauthier a long time?

MME MONNIER: He was my husband's friend before he was anything to me. Since my girlhood in Neuchâtel he has been at our table. He is the oldest friend this house has, Inspector, and I say that as a fact, not a compliment.

MATTHEY: Tell me how the game ended.

MME MONNIER: The doctor said he must go out to fetch his cigars. As he went, he asked me to play for him. I sat down at the piano at once and played until he came back, and I stopped when he came in. I did not look at the clock when he went. I do not look at clocks when I am playing. It is one of the few things I have never needed to be taught.

MATTHEY: What did you play?

MME MONNIER: Chopin. He is the only composer I can play without thinking about my hands, which is why I play him at all.

MATTHEY: Did you hear the hall clock?

MME MONNIER: A moment after he came back, the hall clock struck eleven. The Morbier clock is the only thing in this house that has never once waited for anyone.

MATTHEY: Madame, I am sorry for your loss.

MME MONNIER: Thank you. You may be sorry later, when you have finished with me. I would rather be asked questions than be pitied, if it is all the same to you.

MATTHEY: Very well. You said the doctor is an old friend. Was there any friction between him and your husband?

MME MONNIER: There is friction between any two men who have known each other for thirty years. It is not a crime. It is a marriage, of a sort, between men, and it wears smooth like a stair that everyone climbs.

MATTHEY: And your husband's marriage to you?

MME MONNIER: We were not unhappy. Love wears smooth too, Inspector. It does not stop being love. It stops being something one talks about.

MATTHEY: Félix. Do you know whether he owes money?

MME MONNIER: Félix owes money the way other young men catch colds. He owes more than a young man should, and he thinks charm is a form of credit. My husband told him so. I do not know the amounts, and I have never asked.

MATTHEY: Was there a disagreement at dinner between your husband and Monsieur Girard?

MME MONNIER: Yes. They quarrelled about the repeater, about what Monsieur Girard was prepared to pay for the rights to it. My husband would not sell at a price that insulted four years of work. Monsieur Girard thought the price insulted him. Men of business always think that about a price.

MATTHEY: Did you take any part in it?

MME MONNIER: I poured the wine, Inspector. That was my part.
